# \textit{Alzheimer's Disease and Aging: Aims 1 and 2}

<!-- Name here: -->
Ezra Weible[^1]

[^1]: Biostatistics Masters Student, Colorado School of Public Health, CU Anschutz Medical Campus

Aim 1 evaluate whether peripheral inflammatory markers are associated with a 1 year decline in memory and cortical thickness in aMCI. Hypothesis 1a tests whether baseline cytokine (IL-6, TNF-$\alpha$) and chemokine (MCP-1, Eotaxin-1) levels predict decline. Hypothesis 1b tests whether changes in these markers over the 1 year period are associated with decline. For both hypotheses, the outcome includes AD-signature cortical thickness (continuous). Hypothesis 1a also focuses on memory consolidation (continuous); hypothesis 1b also focuses on five episodic memory outcomes (continuous; (1) 20' Delay, Total Correct, (2) Recognition, D-Prime, (3) 15' Delay, Total Correct, (4) Proportion Correct, (5) 1-Week Delay, Total Correct). All outcomes will be modeled as year 1 values and models will include baseline value adjustments, allowing coefficients to be interpreted as the effect on the 1 year change. For hypothesis 1a, the primary predictor is the baseline cytokine or chemokine value; for hypothesis 1b it is the 1 year change in that marker. Each inflammatory marker will be analyzed in separate models to avoid multicollinearity, with exploratory joint models. The general model form for aim 1 is: $Outcome_{Y1} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Marker_{Y1 \text{ or } Y1-Y0} + \beta_2 Outcome_{Y0} + \beta_n Covariates + \epsilon$ with an alternative hypothesis that $\beta_1 < 0$. 

Aim 2 examines whether amyloid deposition modifies the relationship between inflammation and clinical progression. The primary hypothesis tests whether baseline amyloid deposition interacts with baseline inflammatory markers to predict a one year decline in episodic memory and cortical thickness. The secondary hypothesis tests whether baseline amyloid deposition interacts with the 1 year change in inflammatory markers to predict the one year decline in the outcomes. Models follow a similar approach to aim 1, but include baseline amyloid and an interaction. The general model form for aim 2 is: $Outcome_{Y1} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Marker_{Y1 \text{ or } Y1-Y0} + \beta_2 Amyloid_{Y0} + \beta_3 Marker_{Y1 \text{ or } Y1-Y0} * Amyloid_{Y0} + \beta_4 Outcome_{Y0} + \beta_n Covariates + \epsilon$ with an alternative hypothesis that $\beta_3 < 0$. 

All models will adjust for age, sex, and baseline outcome *a priori*. Data-driven approaches (e.g. LASSO) will be used to identify additional covariates to include that are highly correlated among education, APOE, baseline CDR, GDS,BMI, hypercholesterolemia, blood pressure, NSAID use, immune-related health conditions, and cardiovascular risk. Interpretation will be cautious among correlated variables. For both aims, type I error will be controlled using Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, applied separately within each hypothesis across the different combinations of outcomes and inflammatory markers.

For power, each hypothesis will be approximated using a linear regression framework with a continuous predictor (inflammatory marker or amyloid*marker interaction). Because all longitudinal analyses model year 1 outcomes adjusted for baseline values, we can express the effect of interest as the partial $R^2$ attributable to the predictor of interest. This can be approximated as the squared correlation coefficient (with the effective sample size adjusted for baseline correlation with the year 1 outcome). Power analysis can then be conducted to determine the observable effect size at various power levels with the expected sample size (125 aMCI/50 HC after attrition). This approach will provide a conservative estimate of power, as additional covariates such as age and sex will function as precision variables in the final analysis. Separate power calculations will be performed for each hypothesis.
